pairs.title: The Golden Stairs of the Chilkoot Pass
pairs.thenCaption: The line of stampeders on the last climb to the summit of the Chilkoot Pass, each under a pack, in the winter of 1898.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / E.A. Hegg / CC BY-SA 4.0
pairs.nowCaption: The same slope in summer: a hiker on the Golden Stairs of the Chilkoot Trail, the snow gone and the boulders bare.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Anthony DeLorenzo from Whitehorse, Yukon, Canada / CC BY 2.0
pairs.note: In the winter of 1897–98 the pass carried about 22,000 people and their year's provisions up the Golden Stairs. The railway over the White Pass opened in 1899 and the trail emptied; it is hiked now, in a historic site shared by Parks Canada and the U.S. National Park Service.

pairs.title: Dawson City
pairs.thenCaption: Front Street in the first summer of the rush, a dog team hauling a cart past Jo's Juneau Restaurant, photographed by Eric A. Hegg.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Eric A. Hegg (fl. 1897–1930) / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The Palace Grand Theatre of 1899, rebuilt by Parks Canada in 1962, on King Street two blocks from the river.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Adam Jones, Ph.D. / CC BY-SA 3.0
pairs.note: Seventeen thousand people in the summer of 1898; about 1,500 live in Dawson now. The wooden false fronts and boardwalks are kept or rebuilt by Klondike National Historic Sites, and the river still runs past the end of Front Street.

pairs.title: Miles Canyon
pairs.thenCaption: A stampeders' boat entering the upper end of Miles Canyon in 1898, photographed by Eric A. Hegg.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Eric A. Hegg (fl. 1897–1930) / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The canyon today under the Robert Lowe suspension bridge of 1922, its water slowed by the Whitehorse dam.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / i threw a guitar at him. from United States / CC BY 2.0
pairs.note: Several hundred people drowned here and in the White Horse Rapids below before Sam Steele's police made the rules of 1898. The hydro dam of 1958 drowned the rapids and calmed the canyon.

pairs.title: The graves on Beechey Island
pairs.thenCaption: The graves of three of Franklin's men, found by the search expeditions of 1850–51, drawn for Elisha Kent Kane's narrative.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Kane, Elisha Kent,1820-1857 / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The same graves, with their replacement headboards, on the gravel of Beechey Island.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Ansgar Walk / CC BY-SA 3.0
pairs.note: Franklin's ships wintered here in 1845–46 and left three men in the ground: John Torrington, John Hartnell and William Braine. The site is a territorial historic site of Nunavut; the headboards are replicas of the originals.

pairs.title: Place Royale, Quebec
pairs.thenCaption: Place Royale in the Lower Town of Quebec in 1933, with the church of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires, photographed by Clifford M. Johnston.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Clifford M. Johnston / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: Place Royale in 2017, the square and its stone houses restored to their eighteenth-century lines.
pairs.note: Champlain's Habitation of 1608 stood on this square. The church was begun in 1687 on its site; the square was restored between the 1960s and the 1980s to the appearance of New France.

pairs.title: Fort St. James
pairs.thenCaption: Fort St. James on Stuart Lake, sketched by H. Bullock Webster in 1879.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / H. Bullock Webster / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The fur warehouse of the Hudson's Bay Company's post at Fort St. James National Historic Site.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / JERRYE AND ROY KLOTZ MD / CC BY-SA 3.0
pairs.note: Simon Fraser and John Stuart built the first post here in 1806, in Kwah's country. The buildings standing are the Hudson's Bay Company's of the 1880s, restored by Parks Canada to 1896.

pairs.title: Fort Langley
pairs.thenCaption: The Hudson's Bay Company's Fort Langley on the left bank of the Fraser, with the Langley Buttes beyond, photographed by the boundary survey on 23 September 1858.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Unknown author or not provided / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The palisade gate of Fort Langley National Historic Site, rebuilt on the fort's ground.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Blake Handley from Victoria, Canada / CC BY 2.0
pairs.note: James Douglas took the oath as first governor of British Columbia here on 19 November 1858, weeks after the photograph. One original building, the storehouse of 1840, survives inside the reconstructed palisade.

pairs.title: Fort Edmonton
pairs.thenCaption: Fort Edmonton above the North Saskatchewan, painted by Paul Kane from his visit of 1846.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Paul Kane (1810–1871) / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: A cabin inside the reconstructed fort of 1846 at Fort Edmonton Park.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Dylan Kereluk from White Rock, Canada / CC BY 2.0
pairs.note: The fort Kane painted stood on the river flat below the legislature until 1915. Fort Edmonton Park rebuilt it in the 1970s on a different stretch of the river, to Kane's and the company's records.

pairs.title: Fort William
pairs.thenCaption: The North West Company's Fort William on the Kaministiquia, in a period watercolour held by Library and Archives Canada.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Library and Archives Canada via Commons / Public Domain Mark / PD-Art
pairs.nowCaption: The reconstructed fort at Fort William Historical Park, built upstream of the original site at Pointe de Meuron.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Sajith T S / CC BY-SA 2.0
pairs.note: The original fort of 1803 disappeared under the Canadian Pacific Railway's yards in the 1880s. The reconstruction of the 1970s stands nine miles up the river, with the Great Hall, the palisade and the farm rebuilt to the company's plans.

pairs.title: Upper Fort Garry
pairs.thenCaption: Upper Fort Garry at the Forks of the Red and the Assiniboine, about 1872, in a photograph held by Library and Archives Canada.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Library and Archives Canada via Commons / historical image
pairs.nowCaption: The Governor's Gate of 1853, the one piece of the fort still standing, in Upper Fort Garry Provincial Park in downtown Winnipeg.
pairs.note: Riel's provisional government sat here in 1869–70. The city took the fort down in the 1880s for Main Street; the gate was kept, and the park of 2015 marks the walls' lines in the pavement.

pairs.title: The Lachine Rapids
pairs.thenCaption: The steamer Rapids King shooting the Lachine Rapids in 1901, on a postcard of the day.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Richard from USA / CC BY 2.0
pairs.nowCaption: The rapids today from the Montreal shore, with the Mercier bridge beyond.
pairs.note: The rapids stopped every ship above Montreal; Lachine, above them, was where the canoe brigades loaded. Excursion steamers ran them with Mohawk pilots from Kahnawake for a century; the Lachine Canal of 1825 and the Seaway of 1959 went round them.

pairs.title: Tadoussac
pairs.thenCaption: Tadoussac at the meeting of the Saguenay and the St. Lawrence, in a view published in 1910.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / historical scan / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The Hotel Tadoussac of 1942 on the bay, on the site of the hotel of 1864.
pairs.note: Chauvin's trading post of 1600 stood at the bay, the first French post in Canada; Champlain called here in 1603 and 1608. The whale-watching town of today is on the same cove.

pairs.title: Montreal harbour
pairs.thenCaption: Montreal harbour in 1878, the commercial heart of the fur trade.
pairs.nowCaption: The Old Port today, the quays of the nineteenth century turned to parks and marinas.
pairs.note: The Montreal fur trade shipped its furs from these quays until 1821, and the port grew into Canada's largest through the century that followed. The working port moved downstream in the 1970s and the old quays became the Vieux-Port.

pairs.title: The Habitation at Port-Royal
pairs.thenCaption: The Habitation at Port-Royal as Champlain drew it for his Voyages of 1613.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Samuel de Champlain / CC BY-SA 3.0
pairs.nowCaption: The courtyard and well of the reconstructed Habitation at Port-Royal National Historic Site.
pairs.nowCredit: Wikimedia Commons / CP Hoffman from Washington, DC, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0
pairs.note: De Mons and Champlain built the Habitation in 1605; Argall's Virginians burned it in 1613, the year Champlain's drawing was printed. Parks Canada rebuilt it from the drawing in 1939–41 on the original site, in Membertou's country.

pairs.title: Fort Frontenac
pairs.thenCaption: Fort Frontenac at Cataraqui in 1685, in a plan of the French fort.
pairs.thenCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Unknown author / Public domain
pairs.nowCaption: The uncovered remains of Fort Frontenac's walls in Kingston, beside the Canadian Forces college that holds the site.
pairs.note: Frontenac built the fort in 1673 and La Salle held it as his seigneury; the French demolished it in 1758 before Bradstreet's attack. The British fort and the city of Kingston grew on the ground, and the army still holds it.
